blog1.title: How we built a nonprofit at 15
paras: ElevateX didn’t begin as a structured organization. It began as a response. During board examinations, it became clear how many students around me were dealing with stress, uncertainty, and a lack of accessible support systems.

The initial idea was simple—create something that could help. There was no long-term roadmap, no defined structure, and no expectation of scale. Just small initiatives aimed at solving immediate problems.

But the response changed everything. People didn’t just participate—they stayed. They engaged, contributed, and wanted to be part of something larger. That was the moment it stopped being an idea and started becoming a platform.

The focus then shifted from activity to structure. Instead of doing more, we started building better. Teams were formed, roles were defined, and systems were introduced to ensure continuity. ElevateX evolved from a collection of efforts into something organized and scalable.
One of the most important lessons was that sustainability matters more than speed. Growth without structure breaks. But when systems are in place, growth compounds.
Starting early wasn’t the advantage. Building something that could sustain and evolve—that’s what made the difference.

blog2.title: From Events to Execution
paras: The first fundraiser we organized wasn’t perfect—and it wasn’t supposed to be. Tectonic was never about flawless execution. It was about starting. It exposed gaps we hadn’t anticipated, pressure points we hadn’t prepared for, and the reality that execution is very different from planning.

In theory, everything works. Timelines look clean, responsibilities feel clear, and outcomes seem predictable. But once you actually begin, things shift. Coordination breaks, dependencies appear, and decisions have to be made in real time. That’s where the real learning began.

What followed wasn’t just “more events,” but better systems. Retrograde improved scale. Zenith tested digital execution. Football Fiesta introduced sponsorships and external coordination. And Euphoria pushed everything to its limits—operations, licensing, logistics, and managing people at scale.

The biggest transition was moving from effort to structure. Early on, everything depended on individuals stepping up. Over time, that stopped working. We needed systems—clear roles, defined ownership, and accountability across departments. Planning, finance, marketing—everything had to connect.
Execution is not about intensity in the moment. It’s about preparation before it and systems behind it. That’s what creates consistency. That’s what allows something to scale without breaking.
Looking back, events weren’t the goal. They were the training ground. The real outcome was learning how to build something that actually works under pressure—and keeps working as it grows.

blog3.title: Why Financial Literacy Matters
paras: Financial literacy is one of the most practical skills a student can develop, yet it remains largely absent from formal education. Students are taught complex theories, but rarely how to manage money, assess risk, or make informed financial decisions.
This gap becomes visible very quickly. People enter adulthood without understanding saving, investing, or even basic financial planning. The consequences aren’t immediate—but they compound over time.
The issue isn’t lack of intelligence. It’s lack of exposure. Financial concepts are often seen as advanced or optional, when in reality they are foundational to everyday life.
Project Unnati was created to address this gap—not through traditional teaching, but through practical learning. The goal was to make financial concepts accessible, relevant, and directly applicable.
Instead of focusing on theory, the emphasis was on understanding—how money works, how decisions affect outcomes, and how small actions compound over time.
Financial awareness changes behavior. And when introduced early, it creates long-term impact that extends far beyond academics.

blog4.title: From Member to Leadership: My Journey at ElevateX
paras: I joined ElevateX last year as a general member, beginning my journey in the Drive Execution Team. During this time, I actively participated in multiple drives and contributed consistently to their smooth and efficient execution.

Beyond my assigned responsibilities, I took initiative to deepen my involvement by understanding how operations functioned at a broader level. One of the most defining experiences during this phase was independently hosting a drive. Taking full ownership of an initiative strengthened my leadership, planning, and organizational abilities while pushing me beyond my comfort zone.

Recognizing my dedication and performance, I was promoted to an Executive Member (X Member), and subsequently took on the role of Head of the Drive Execution Team. In this capacity, my responsibilities expanded from execution to leadership. I was involved in planning initiatives, coordinating with team members, and ensuring that each project was delivered efficiently and to a high standard.

This year, I also played a key role in organizing our flagship event, the Winterland Carnival, “Euphoria.” As a core committee member, I was responsible for securing sponsors and onboarding multiple stalls, both of which were critical to the scale and success of the event.

In addition, I served as the Head of Security for the event. This role required managing safety protocols, coordinating security arrangements, and ensuring a smooth and secure experience for all attendees. It demanded attention to detail, quick decision-making, and strong coordination throughout the event.

My journey at ElevateX has been incredibly enriching. It has enabled me to develop essential skills in leadership, teamwork, communication, and event management, while also building the confidence to take initiative and handle responsibilities at a much larger scale.

ElevateX has provided me with an environment where growth is not just encouraged, but expected — an environment where individuals are trusted with responsibility and given the opportunity to learn through real experience.

founder.title: Founder’s Note
paras: ElevateX didn’t begin as a large organization. It began as a simple frustration.

I kept seeing student-led initiatives with strong intent but no continuity. There was energy, there were ideas — but most of it stayed temporary. A few events, a few drives, and then it faded. There was no system to sustain or scale what was being built.
ElevateX was built to change that.

When Samridh, Devyansh and I began working on this, we didn’t expect it to become what it is today. On 8th March, when ElevateX officially came into existence, it was still just an idea we were trying to make work — nothing more.
From the beginning, the focus was clear. Not on doing more, but on building something that could last.
Structure was one part of that. Systems, roles, processes — things that allow work to continue without depending on a few people.
But structure alone doesn’t build an organization.
What truly defines ElevateX is its culture.

The late-night meetings after work was done. The conversations that had nothing to do with tasks. The inside jokes, the stickers, the countless WhatsApp groups that made this feel less like an obligation and more like a space people wanted to be in.
Those small, almost insignificant moments — they are what built this.
Because when people feel like they belong, they stay. And when they stay, they build.
There were moments where this could have fallen apart.
An internal conflict that could have broken the organization entirely. A night before an event where the venue was cancelled last minute, and everything we had worked for was at risk.
But it didn’t collapse.
People stepped in. Not because they had to — but because they felt responsible for what this was.
That is the difference.
Most student organizations don’t fail because of lack of ideas. They fail because there is nothing that holds people together.
ElevateX works because people don’t feel like they are working for it. They feel like it belongs to them.
From the start, the approach was simple — give individuals ownership. Not in theory, but in practice. This is your organization. Build what you want to build. Take responsibility for it.
That is what scaled ElevateX.
Not just events or initiatives, but people who were willing to take ownership and carry things forward.
For me, ElevateX has been more than just an organization. It has completely changed how I think, how I work, and who I am.
And that is what I want this to become for others.
Not just a place to participate, but a place that changes people — in ways that stay long after they leave.
This is still a work in progress.
And that is exactly how it should be.
— Vivaan Agarwal
Founder, ElevateX

founder2.title: Founder’s Note
paras: What matters isn’t what you start — it’s what continues without you.
From the beginning, ElevateX was never approached as just an initiative. It was something that needed to function properly — something that could sustain itself beyond individual effort.
Ideas were always present. The real challenge was execution.

The focus, therefore, was on building how things run — creating structure, defining clear responsibilities, and ensuring that work didn’t depend on last-minute effort or a few individuals stepping in to fix problems.
Because without structure, growth doesn’t strengthen an organization — it only exposes its weaknesses.

As ElevateX expanded into larger projects, expectations evolved quickly. Timelines became stricter, coordination more demanding, and accountability non-negotiable. This shift required operating with greater clarity, discipline, and consistency.
There were moments — across events and fundraising — where things didn’t go as planned. Yet, outcomes were delivered. More importantly, they were delivered without collapse.
That was the real validation.
It showed that the system was working.
That is what ElevateX stands on today.
Not just ideas, but execution that holds up over time.
A structure where individuals can step in, take ownership, and build something meaningful — without dependence on any single person.
Still evolving. Still improving.
And that is exactly how it should be.
— Devyansh Tolasaria
Founder, ElevateX

founder3.title: Founder’s Note
paras: Hi, I’m Samridh, one of the founding members of ELEVATE-X.

The story of ELEVATE-X begins on the night of 16th December 2024, when Vivaan called me and proposed the idea of starting a nonprofit organisation. The concept was still in its early stages, yet it was driven by a clear sense of purpose and passion.

In the midst of our pre-board examinations, Vivaan, Devyansh, and I began working on ELEVATE-X, dedicating countless late nights to turning our vision into reality. On 8th March, ELEVATE-X officially came into existence.

We founded ELEVATE-X as a teen-led nonprofit with the objective of providing young minds with hands-on experience in areas such as finance, execution, and operations, while simultaneously contributing to the betterment of society.
The organisation was designed to bridge the gap between academic learning and real-world impact, empowering students to apply their skills in meaningful ways.

In my role as CFO, I gained valuable experience in financial management, risk mitigation, and strategic planning. I was responsible for overseeing fundraising initiatives, managing organisational funds, and ensuring that each campaign remained financially sustainable.
This experience not only strengthened my technical skills but also deepened my sense of accountability and responsibility toward the organisation’s mission.
ELEVATE-X, to me, represents a community of like-minded individuals who are committed to creating positive change in both their own lives and in society.
If you possess the drive and dedication to contribute to a better future, ELEVATE-X offers a structured, purpose-driven platform to begin your journey.
— Samridh Sanganeria
Founder, ElevateX
